key_terms.meaning: A self-generating sensor that converts the measurand directly into electrical energy, such as a thermocouple or piezoelectric sensor.
A sensor that needs an external supply and changes its resistance, capacitance or inductance when the measurand changes.
The physical quantity being measured, such as temperature, pressure or strain.
A device that converts an electrical signal back into a physical quantity, such as a loudspeaker or actuator.
Change of a material's resistance when it is mechanically strained; used in strain gauges and pressure sensors.
Production of an emf in a circuit of two dissimilar metals whose junctions are at different temperatures; the basis of a thermocouple.
The documented comparison of a sensor's output with a reference standard of known uncertainty.
An unbroken chain of calibrations, each with stated uncertainty, linking the sensor to a national or international standard.
How close the measured value is to the true value; a qualitative statement of total error.
How closely repeated readings agree with one another under the same conditions; also called repeatability.
The smallest change of input that produces a detectable change in output.
The change of output divided by the change of input, S = Δy/Δx.
How closely the sensor's calibration curve follows a straight line over its range.
The difference in output for the same input when approached from increasing and decreasing directions.
For a first-order sensor, the time to reach 63.2% of the final output after a step input; τ = RC or m c / (h A).
For a second-order sensor, the ratio of actual damping to critical damping; it sets overshoot and ringing.
The undamped frequency at which a second-order sensor would oscillate freely.
A repeatable error that shifts all readings in the same direction, also called bias.
A scatter in repeated readings that varies unpredictably; reduced by averaging.
A parameter that characterises the range of values within which the true value is expected to lie.

takeaways: Active sensors generate their own electrical signal; passive sensors need an external excitation supply and modify it.
Every sensor rests on a physical law that converts the measurand into a change of resistance, capacitance, inductance or emf.
Calibration is a documented comparison against a traceable standard, not just an adjustment of the zero knob.
Static characteristics answer different questions: accuracy is closeness to truth, precision is repeatability, and resolution is the smallest detectable change.
Linearity, hysteresis and drift describe how far a real sensor departs from an ideal straight-line response.
First-order sensors lag with a time constant τ; second-order sensors add overshoot and ringing set by damping ratio ζ and natural frequency ωₙ.
Error analysis separates systematic bias from random scatter and reports a best estimate with an uncertainty.
A measurement chain from sensor to display must be analysed as a system, because each block adds its own error and lag.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine sensor classification, static and dynamic characteristics and error analysis, with a worked numerical example and a clear statement of assumptions.

bank.q: Compare active and passive sensors. Explain how the classification decides wiring and signal conditioning, and give two examples of each.
outline: Define active and passive sensors with self-generating and externally energised behaviour.
Examples: thermocouple and piezoelectric sensor as active; strain gauge and thermistor as passive.
Active sensors need no excitation but may need high-impedance amplifiers.
Passive sensors need a stable supply and a bridge or divider circuit.
Mention output form and typical signal-conditioning blocks.

bank.q: State four physical principles used in sensors. Explain how each converts a measurand into an electrical quantity.
outline: Variable resistance: strain gauge, thermistor.
Variable capacitance: parallel-plate capacitive pressure sensor.
Variable inductance: LVDT or reluctance sensor.
Thermoelectric emf: thermocouple.
Piezoelectric charge: piezoelectric accelerometer.
For each, name the physical law and the electrical output.

bank.q: Explain calibration, verification, adjustment and traceability. Why is traceability necessary in a calibration record?
outline: Calibration: comparison with a standard and recording results.
Verification: checking that the instrument meets a specification.
Adjustment: physical change to bring output closer to the true value.
Traceability: unbroken chain of comparisons with stated uncertainties to a national standard.
Traceability makes readings legally and technically defensible.

bank.q: Define accuracy, precision, resolution, sensitivity, linearity, span, range and dead band. Give one practical example of each.
outline: Accuracy versus precision with a target analogy.
Resolution as smallest detectable input change.
Sensitivity as Δy/Δx with units.
Linearity as maximum deviation from a best-fit or end-point straight line.
Span = ymax − ymin; range = input limits.
Dead band as input change that produces no output change.

bank.q: Distinguish systematic, random and gross errors. Define absolute error, relative error and percentage error.
outline: Systematic error or bias: repeatable shift, correctable by calibration.
Random error: scatter, reduced by averaging and statistics.
Gross error or blunder: human mistake, rejected, not averaged.
Absolute error = measured − true, with units.
Relative error = absolute error / true value.
Percentage error = relative error × 100%.

bank.q: A passive sensor has resistance 500 Ω at 0 kPa and 520 Ω at 100 kPa. It is connected in a voltage divider with a 500 Ω series resistor and a 5 V supply. Calculate the output at 0 kPa and at 100 kPa, and the sensitivity in mV/kPa.
outline: Use Vout = 5 × R / (R + 500).
At 0 kPa: Vout = 2.500 V.
Change = 0.049 V = 49 mV.
Sensitivity = 49 mV / 100 kPa = 0.49 mV/kPa.
State that the response is nonlinear and sensitivity is an average over the range.

bank.q: A calibration table gives increasing and decreasing readings for a pressure sensor. Explain how to compute span, average sensitivity, hysteresis and maximum linearity error from the table.
outline: Span = full-scale output − zero output.
Average sensitivity = span / input span.
Hysteresis = maximum difference between increasing and decreasing outputs at the same input.
Linearity error: compare output with a best-fit or end-point straight line.
Express each error in output units and as a percentage of span.
Draw a labelled calibration curve.

bank.q: A first-order temperature sensor has a time constant of 2 s. It is suddenly placed in a bath whose temperature steps by 40 °C. Find the output at 2 s, the time to reach 95% of the step, and the reading error at 10 s.
outline: First-order step response: y(t) = A(1 − e^(−t/τ)).
At t = τ = 2 s, output reaches 63.2% of 40 °C = 25.3 °C.
For 95%, t = 3τ = 6 s.
Reading error = 40 × e^(−5) = 0.27 °C.
State assumptions: single time constant, no self-heating.

bank.q: A second-order accelerometer has natural frequency 100 rad/s and damping ratio 0.2. Calculate the percentage overshoot and peak time for a step input, and comment on its usable frequency range.
outline: Percentage overshoot = 100 × e^(−πζ / √(1 − ζ²)).
For ζ = 0.2, overshoot ≈ 52.7%.
Peak time = π / (ωₙ√(1 − ζ²)) ≈ 0.032 s.
Low damping causes severe ringing near resonance.
For flat response, use ω well below ωₙ and prefer ζ near 0.6 to 0.8.
Sketch the step response.

bank.q: Ten repeated readings of a voltage are 5.01, 4.99, 5.00, 5.02, 4.98, 5.00, 5.01, 4.99, 5.00 and 5.00 V. Calculate the mean, sample standard deviation, standard error and a 95% confidence interval.
outline: Mean = 5.000 V.
Compute deviations and sample standard deviation s.
Standard error = s / √n with n = 10.
95% confidence interval uses t ≈ 2.262 for 9 degrees of freedom.
Report result as mean ± expanded uncertainty with units.
Separate random uncertainty from any systematic calibration bias.

bank.q: A parcel-weighing scale for a UPI payment counter must measure loads from 0.1 kg to 20 kg with 5 g resolution. Choose a sensing principle, justify active or passive operation, and evaluate the static characteristics needed.
outline: Load cell with strain gauges as a passive Wheatstone bridge sensor.
Justify: linear, repeatable, rugged and available in low-profile platforms.
Resolution depends on bridge excitation, amplifier gain and ADC bits.
Accuracy must include hysteresis, creep and temperature drift.
Calibration with standard masses and traceability.
Discuss wiring, shielding and signal conditioning.

bank.q: A calibration report shows zero drift of 0.5% span, hysteresis of 1% span and a linearity error of 0.8% span over a 0–200 kPa range. Evaluate whether the sensor suits a process needing ±1.5 kPa accuracy.
outline: Convert each error to kPa: span = 200 kPa.
Zero drift = 1.0 kPa; hysteresis = 2.0 kPa; linearity = 1.6 kPa.
Hysteresis alone exceeds the ±1.5 kPa limit.
Combine errors in the worst case and by root-sum-square.
Recommend recalibration, a better sensor or reduced range.
State that accuracy is not the same as resolution.

bank.q: A first-order sensor with time constant τ measures a ramp input of slope k. Derive the steady-state lag error and evaluate how τ affects the reading during a fast temperature rise.
outline: Model τ dy/dt + y = x(t), with x = kt.
Steady-state solution gives y = k(t − τ).
Lag error = kτ, proportional to slope and time constant.
Smaller τ gives smaller dynamic error.
For a step change, the error decays as e^(−t/τ).
Recommend sensor selection based on the fastest expected ramp.

bank.q: Compare piezoresistive and capacitive MEMS pressure sensors for a tyre-pressure monitor. Consider sensitivity, temperature drift, power, size and signal conditioning.
outline: Piezoresistive: Wheatstone bridge, simple readout, moderate sensitivity, temperature drift.
Capacitive: high sensitivity, low power, needs capacitance-to-voltage circuitry.
Both can be micromachined and made small.
Tyre monitor needs wide temperature range and long battery life.
Evaluate drift, packaging and calibration cost.
Give a reasoned choice with trade-offs.

glossary.def: A device that responds to a physical quantity and produces a measurable output.
A device that converts one form of energy into another, often a physical quantity into an electrical signal.
A device that converts an electrical signal into a physical action or quantity.
A self-generating sensor that produces an electrical output without an external excitation supply.
A sensor whose electrical property changes with the measurand and which needs an external supply.
The physical quantity that a sensor is intended to measure.
A transducer that converts an electrical signal back into a non-electrical physical quantity.
The process of comparing a sensor's output with a reference standard and recording the result.
A documented chain of comparisons linking a measurement to a recognised standard.
Checking that an instrument meets a stated specification or requirement.
A physical or software change made to bring an instrument's output closer to the true value.
The closeness of a measured value to the true value.
The closeness of repeated measurements to one another.
The smallest input change that produces a detectable output change.
The ratio of output change to input change, S = Δy/Δx.
The closeness of a sensor's calibration curve to a straight line.
The difference between output readings for the same input when approached from opposite directions.
A slow change in output with time or ambient conditions when the input is constant.
The difference between the maximum and minimum output over the specified range.
The lower and upper limits of input over which a sensor is specified to operate.
The range of input change that produces no detectable change in output.
The time for a first-order sensor to reach 63.2% of its final response to a step input.
The ratio of actual damping to critical damping in a second-order system.
A repeatable error that shifts all readings by the same amount or in the same direction.
An unpredictable scatter in repeated readings that can be reduced by averaging.
A quantified range around a measured value within which the true value is expected to lie.
